APR4qSB0W9c.title: Inside America's Biggest Emergency Highway Project
APR4qSB0W9c.desc:
In 2024, Hurricane Helene washed portions of Interstate 40 into the Pigeon River, severing a critical connection between North Carolina and Tennessee. Now, crews are undertaking an enormous emergency reconstruction project designed to make sure it doesn't happen again. 

We traveled to western North Carolina with Ames Construction to see how they're rebuilding I-40 inside a narrow mountain gorge where floodwaters completely erased sections of the highway.

At the center of the project is the ARC, a massive wall built from roller-compacted concrete (RCC). During another major flood, the structure is designed to deflect the Pigeon River away from the rebuilt interstate. But the ARC is only one part of the solution. Nearly 400,000 linear feet of interlocking pipe piles help protect against scour, while a massive temporary soil-nail wall stabilizes the remaining highway carrying traffic above the construction site. 

The scale of the operation gets even crazier behind the scenes. Ames established a temporary quarry specifically for the project, where crews blast and excavate roughly 1.5 million cubic yards of rock. An enormous crushing operation then processes material for the two on-site RCC batch plants, eliminating the need for hundreds of thousands of over-the-road truckloads.

Then, every night, the real action begins.

Thousands of yards of RCC travel down the gorge before specialized equipment places the material in one-foot lifts, almost like a giant concrete 3D printer. By the end of the project, crews will have placed roughly 800,000 cubic yards of roller-compacted concrete to help protect the new interstate from future flooding.

Hurricane Helene took only days to destroy the highway. Rebuilding it to withstand the next major flood will take years of around-the-clock work.

vfIaNeGVaVo.title: Nepal's 2026 Disaster Explained: The Glacier That Wiped Out a Valley
vfIaNeGVaVo.desc:
Most coverage of this disaster starts in the valley.
This video starts four thousand metres above it, because that is where the thing that destroyed those villages began, and because what left the mountain and what arrived at the bottom were not the same size.
That difference is the entire story.

A mass of rock and ice detaches at high altitude. It falls. On the way down, friction converts its own ice into water, and what began as a rockfall stops behaving like rock and starts behaving like a fluid. Then it travels, and as it travels it scours the valley beneath it, tearing up moraine, sediment, boulders, trees and river water and absorbing all of it.

It arrives at settlements many times larger than the mass that originally fell.

The valley did not just carry the flow. The valley fed it.
That is why survivors of these events describe hearing something before they saw anything, and why what reached the villages was not a flood in any ordinary sense. A debris flow is majority solid material by volume, closer to wet concrete than to water. It carries boulders. It does not inundate buildings, it strikes them. In the highest energy sections it removes the ground itself.

WHAT THIS VIDEO EXPLAINS
Why permafrost, not rock strength, is what holds high Himalayan slopes together
What actually happens to a falling rock and ice mass on the way down
Entrainment, and why these flows multiply in volume as they descend
Why a debris flow destroys structures a river flood would leave standing
Why warning times in steep valleys are measured in minutes
Why landslide-dammed lakes mean the danger does not end when the flow stops
What the 2021 Chamoli disaster taught researchers, and why they expected another

A NOTE ON THIS VIDEO
Figures for this event have been revised repeatedly and are still changing. Every number shown on screen carries the date and source it came from. Where the science is not yet settled, this video says so rather than filling the gap.
There is no reconstruction footage of people here and no casualty figure in the thumbnail. The mechanism is the subject. People are still missing and their families are still waiting.

SOURCES AND FURTHER READING
ICIMOD, Kathmandu, for Himalayan hazard research
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority for official figures
Published work on the 2021 Chamoli rock-ice avalanche, the closest documented precedent
Peer reviewed literature on high mountain permafrost degradation

00:00 - The Morning of August 26, 2026

Deadly floods are hitting Texas Hill Country again in July 2026. But why does the same weather pattern create such dangerous flash floods again and again? Watch this video to find out why this river is so deadly.

After the 2025 Central Texas floods, one question remains: why is the Guadalupe still the most dangerous river in America? We go inside the "Flash Flood Alley" to see the hidden mechanics of a modern flood disaster and the tech working to keep your community safe.

Why is the Guadalupe River the most dangerous river in the US? Hidden in the heart of "Flash Flood Alley," the Guadalupe River holds a lethal secret. While the US map is dotted with flood zones, a shocking statistical anomaly exists over Central Texas—a "deadly cluster" where the geography of the Hill Country meets the volatile energy of the Gulf of Mexico.

In this episode of Weathered, host Maiya May dives into the science of "Impossible Rain" and the "Rain Bombs" that fueled the devastating 2025 Central Texas Floods. We explore why the Guadalupe is uniquely prone to transforming into a racing wall of water with almost no warning, and how superheated Gulf air is changing the math on what a "100-year flood" actually looks like.

In this episode, we break down:

The Geography of Danger: Why the Texas Hill Country acts as a funnel for catastrophic surges.

The 2025 Impact: A look at the data behind the recent deadly July flooding.

The Science of "Impossible Rain": How a warming climate is supercharging local weather patterns.

Saving Lives: The new tower-based monitoring systems and early-warning research being deployed to predict the unpredictable.

From meteorologists to real-time flood researchers, meet the people working to prevent deaths along this underestimated river basin.
